metadata.title: Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions

nodes.name: Positional population count (multiple-sum problem)
nodes.statement: Given a stream of $k$-bit words, we seek to compute $k$~distinct sums corresponding to bit values at indexes 0, 1, 2, \ldots, $k-1$. If the $k$-bit words are one-hot encoded then the sums correspond to a frequency histogram.
nodes.statement_short: Compute, for a stream of $k$-bit words, the $k$ per-position sums of set bits (a frequency histogram for one-hot input).

nodes.name: Abstract performance claim for the SIMD positional population count
nodes.statement: Using SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions from recent Intel processors, we describe algorithms for computing the 16-bit position population count using less than half of a CPU cycle per 16-bit word. Our best approach uses up to 400~times fewer instructions and is up to 50~times faster than baseline code using only regular (non-SIMD) instructions, for sufficiently large inputs.
nodes.statement_short: SIMD pospopcnt runs at under half a cycle per 16-bit word, up to 400x fewer instructions and 50x faster than scalar code.
assumptions: for sufficiently large inputs
conclusions: computing the 16-bit position population count using less than half of a CPU cycle per 16-bit word
Our best approach uses up to 400~times fewer instructions and is up to 50~times faster than baseline code using only regular (non-SIMD) instructions

nodes.name: Population count (popcnt, Hamming weight, sideways sum)
nodes.statement: In many applications such as deep learning\cite{Dai2017,Courbariaux2016,Zhang2018,Hubara2016}, indexing\cite{Lemire2016}, chemistry\cite{Haque2011}, cryptography\cite{Sanyal2018}, and bioinformatics\cite{Layer2016,Danek2018,Wu2010,Purcell2007} it is desirable to compute the number of set bits in a computer word. This operation is referred to as the population count (\texttt{popcnt}), Hamming weight, or the sideways sum of the word.
nodes.statement_short: The population count of a word is its number of set bits.
nodes.definiendum: population count (\texttt{popcnt}), Hamming weight, or the sideways sum of the word
differentia: compute the number of set bits in a computer word

nodes.name: Population count of 10010010
nodes.statement: For example, the machine word \texttt{\underline{1}00\underline{1}00\underline{1}0} has a population count of three since there are three set bits.

nodes.name: One-hot (1-of-$k$) encoding
nodes.statement: It is common to represent categorical variables using one-hot (1-of-$k$) encoding\cite{lippert2013exhaustive,mittag2015influence} where each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word and each word may only have a single bit set.
nodes.origin_citation: Lippert et al. 2013; Mittag et al. 2015
differentia: each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word
each word may only have a single bit set

nodes.name: One-hot encoded \texttt{country} variable and its frequency histogram
nodes.statement: As an illustrative example, consider a categorical variable \texttt{country} that has the eight distinct values \texttt{Australia}, \texttt{Canada}, \texttt{China}, \texttt{France}, \texttt{Japan}, \texttt{Portugal}, \texttt{Spain}, and \texttt{USA}. These categorical string values can be unambiguously dictionary-compressed into one-hot encodings (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample}) resulting in lower memory usage and more efficient queries. One of the motivations for such categorical encodings is that many machine-learning algorithms require numerical variables and cannot operate directly on categorical data. These encodings are closely related to the concept of dummy variables in statistics where categorical attributes are represented as zeros or ones for computing purposes. In this context, we want to compute the frequency histogram, that is the number of occurrences of each value. For example, given a stream (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample-stream}) of one-hot encoded values (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample}), we want to compute the number of times each country has been observed such that \texttt{France} has been observed three times, \texttt{Portugal} two times, \texttt{USA} four times, and \texttt{China} one time.
nodes.statement_short: Eight countries one-hot encoded into a byte; counting a stream of such bytes yields the per-country frequency histogram.

nodes.name: Positional population count (pospopcnt)
nodes.statement: We name this novel generalization of the population count operation to individual bits spanning multiple words as the \textit{positional population count} (\texttt{pospopcnt}). If each word is made of $k$-bits then we want to compute $k$~counts representing the total number of set bits at each of the $k$~positions.
nodes.statement_short: The pospopcnt of a stream of $k$-bit words is the vector of $k$ counts of set bits, one per bit position.
nodes.genus: generalization of the population count operation
differentia: to individual bits spanning multiple words
we want to compute $k$~counts representing the total number of set bits at each of the $k$~positions

nodes.name: Three input words $A$, $B$, $C$: per-word versus positional population count
nodes.statement: As an illustrative example, consider three given input words $A$, $B$, and $C$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:introduction}), the conventional per-word population count computes the number of set bits for each word independently (Fig.~\ref{fig:introductionpane2}). In contrast, the positional population count operation computes the \emph{vertical} population count over these words for independent bit positions (Fig.~\ref{fig:introductionpane1}).
nodes.statement_short: Contrasts horizontal (per-word) popcount with the vertical, per-bit-position pospopcnt on three words.

nodes.name: Main contribution and 50-fold speedup claim
nodes.statement: Our main contribution is the formalized description of the novel positional population count operation and the introduction of an efficient algorithmic family for computing it using SIMD instructions leveraging the AVX-512 instruction set architecture (ISA) available on recent Intel processors. The AVX-512 family of ISAs can operate on up to thirty-two 512-bit registers. Notably, we show that our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach, as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes).
nodes.statement_short: Contribution: formalize pospopcnt and give an AVX-512 algorithmic family over 50x faster than scalar for large inputs.
assumptions: as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes)
conclusions: our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach

nodes.name: Absence of prior work on the positional population count
nodes.statement: To our knowledge, there is no prior work in the literature describing the positional population count. In contrast, computation of the population count has enjoyed renewed interest\cite{mula2017faster} following recent advancements in hardware with wider registers and more diverse and mature instruction-set architectures. Computing the population count is of such general importance that most commodity processors have dedicated instructions (e.g. \texttt{popcnt} on x64 processors). These hardware instructions are efficient when operating on single words. When large volumes of machine words are available in contiguous memory, other software-based approaches have demonstrated superior performance\cite{mula2017faster}.
nodes.statement_short: No prior literature on pospopcnt; by contrast popcount is well studied and hardware-supported.

nodes.name: Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population-count (tree of adders)
nodes.statement: One of the earliest efficient algorithm to compute the population count is the Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population-count\cite{Wilkes} (Fig.~\ref{fig:tree-of-adders}). This algorithm begins by adding adjacent bits into two-bit subwords, then adds these two-bit subwords into four-bit subwords, and finally adds adjacent four-bit subwords into byte values. These byte values are then summed using a multiplication and a bit-shift. It has a natural tree structure and can be described as a "tree of adders"\cite{KnuthV4A}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute a word's popcount by a tree of adders: pairwise bit sums widened to 2-, 4-, then 8-bit subwords, finally summed by multiply-and-shift.
nodes.origin_citation: Wilkes, Wheeler & Gill; Knuth TAOCP V4A

nodes.statement: This algorithm begins by adding adjacent bits into two-bit subwords,
nodes.statement_short: Pairwise-sum adjacent bits into 2-bit fields.

nodes.statement: then adds these two-bit subwords into four-bit subwords,
nodes.statement_short: Widen the partial sums to 4-bit fields.

nodes.statement: and finally adds adjacent four-bit subwords into byte values.
nodes.statement_short: Widen the partial sums to byte fields.

nodes.name: Sum the byte values with a multiplication and a bit-shift

nodes.name: Carry-save adder (CSA) subroutine
nodes.statement: Another efficient approach\cite{warren2007} is the Harley-Seal algorithm that is based on carry-save adder (CSA) networks frequently used in hardware microarchitectures. The CSA subroutine takes three input words and produce two output words: (1) a sequence of partial sum bits, and (2) a sequence of carry bits.
nodes.statement_short: A CSA maps three input words to two output words: partial sums and carries.
nodes.genus: subroutine [that] takes three input words and produce two output words
differentia: a sequence of partial sum bits

nodes.name: Three-bit sum via 5 logical operations
nodes.statement: Given three~bit values ($a,b,c\in \{0,1\}$), the sum $a + b + c$ is computed as a 2-bit word where the least significant bit is given by $(a\bitwisexor b) \bitwisexor c$ and the most significant bit is given by $(a \bitwiseand b) \bitwiseor ( (a \bitwisexor b) \bitwiseand c )$. We reuse the $a \bitwisexor b$ expression from the computation of the least significant bit when computing the most significant bit. Therefore, three values can be summed using 5~logical operations.
nodes.statement_short: The 2-bit sum of three bits is given by xor/and/or formulas costing 5 logical operations once $a\,\mathrm{xor}\,b$ is shared.
assumptions: Given three~bit values ($a,b,c\in \{0,1\}$)
conclusions: the least significant bit is given by $(a\bitwisexor b) \bitwisexor c$
the most significant bit is given by $(a \bitwiseand b) \bitwiseor ( (a \bitwisexor b) \bitwiseand c )$
three values can be summed using 5~logical operations

nodes.name: CSA (bitwise parallel carry-save adder, 64-bit C++)
nodes.statement_short: 64-bit-parallel carry-save adder: five bitwise operations produce the high and low bits of $a+b+c$.
nodes.origin_citation: Warren 2007 (Harley-Seal); code as given by this paper
input: uint64_t a, uint64_t b, uint64_t c

nodes.name: Compute the shared xor
nodes.statement: uint64_t u = a xor b;
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the shared temporary $u = a\,\mathrm{xor}\,b$.

nodes.name: Compute the most significant bits
nodes.statement: *h = (a bitand b) bitor (u bitand c);
nodes.statement_short: Write the carry (high) word.

nodes.name: Compute the least significant bits
nodes.statement: *l = u xor c;
nodes.statement_short: Write the partial-sum (low) word.

nodes.name: Harley-Seal CSA circuit for four input words
nodes.statement: Starting with two 64-bit words initialized to zero: one for the least significant bits ($B_0$) and one for the second least significant bits ($B_1$). \begin{enumerate} \item Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$. \item Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$. \item In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Three CSA calls reduce four input words plus running counters $B_0,B_1$ to bit-plane words $B_0,B_1,B_2$.

nodes.name: First CSA on two inputs and $B_0$
nodes.statement: Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA the first two inputs into $B_0$, producing carry $x$.

nodes.name: Second CSA on two further inputs and $B_0$
nodes.statement: Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA the next two inputs into $B_0$, producing carry $y$.

nodes.name: Combine the two carries with $B_1$
nodes.statement: In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA $x$, $y$ and $B_1$ to update $B_1$ and emit $B_2$.

nodes.name: Weighted recombination of bit-plane population counts
nodes.statement: If $c_i$ is the population count of $B_i$, then the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$. In general, given $2^N$~input words, we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit. Then the per-word population count can be computed from the resulting $N$~words.
nodes.statement_short: Popcounts of the bit-plane words recombine with weights $1,2,4,\ldots$ to give the total popcount.
assumptions: If $c_i$ is the population count of $B_i$
given $2^N$~input words
conclusions: the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$
we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit

nodes.name: $2^N-1$ CSA routines suffice for $2^N$ inputs
nodes.statement: By such a recursive argument, we can show that $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs.
nodes.statement_short: A CSA circuit on $2^N$ inputs can be built from $2^N-1$ CSA routines.
assumptions: $2^N$~inputs
conclusions: $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs

nodes.name: Recursive doubling construction of CSA circuits
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a circuit that takes $2^N$~inputs as well as $B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1}$ and produces the updated $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$ corresponding to the sum. We can represent this circuit as a function $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$ that outputs $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$. We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine. Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$. We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$. We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $N$: build $F_{N+1}$ from two calls to $F_N$ plus one extra CSA combining the three copies of $B_N$.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis: the circuit $F_N$
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a circuit that takes $2^N$~inputs as well as $B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1}$ and produces the updated $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$ corresponding to the sum. We can represent this circuit as a function $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$ that outputs $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the induction hypothesis and name the $2^N$-input circuit $F_N$.

nodes.name: Doubling strategy
nodes.statement: We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: State the inductive step: two $F_N$ calls plus one CSA give $F_{N+1}$.

nodes.name: Chain two calls to $F_N$
nodes.statement: Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$. We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Feed the first call's outputs into a second $F_N$ call on the remaining $2^N$ inputs.

nodes.name: Combine the three $B_N$ values
nodes.statement: We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Merge the three surviving $B_N$ words with one extra CSA.

nodes.name: SIMD parallelization of the CSA circuit
nodes.statement: In addition to being scaled to more inputs, the CSA circuit can be be parallelized using wide SIMD registers (e.g. 512-bit words using the AVX-512 ISA). Instead of processing 64-bit words one-by-one, we can process multiple 64-bit words in parallel resulting in greater speed. Given sufficiently large input arrays (e.g., 1\,kB), such a SIMD-accelerated CSA network is superior to all known population count alternatives on current Intel processors\cite{mula2017faster}.
nodes.statement_short: Widening the CSA circuit to SIMD registers makes it the fastest known popcount for large arrays.

nodes.name: Related constructions in cryptography
nodes.statement: Furthermore, our general strategy and many of our constructions are familiar to cryptographers~\cite{chou2016qcbits}. Some of these researchers have produced related optimizations using advanced SIMD instructions~\cite{guimaraes2019optimized,drucker2020qc}.
nodes.origin_citation: Chou 2016; Guimarães et al. 2019; Drucker et al. 2020

nodes.name: Two-instruction CSA using \texttt{vpternlogd}
nodes.statement: The conventional approach for computing the CSA routine requires 5~logical operations. On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available, we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd} using the \texttt{\_mm512\_ternarylogic\_epi32} intrinsic function (Fig.~\ref{fig:csa-avx512}).
nodes.statement_short: AVX-512's ternary-logic instruction reduces the CSA from 5 logical operations to 2 instructions.
assumptions: On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available
conclusions: we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd}

nodes.name: \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction
nodes.statement: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$ and returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$.
differentia: operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$
returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$

nodes.name: \texttt{vpternlogd} computes any ternary Boolean function
nodes.statement: Given three 512-bit input registers, the instructions generates a 512-bit output, executing 512-bit operations in parallel. The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction.
nodes.statement_short: One \texttt{vpternlogd} evaluates an arbitrary 3-input Boolean function across 512 bits in parallel.
assumptions: Given three 512-bit input registers
conclusions: the instructions generates a 512-bit output, executing 512-bit operations in parallel
The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction

nodes.name: Ternary-logic constants 150 and 232 for the CSA routine
nodes.statement: To determine the value of the 8-bit sequence $i$ in the context of computing the least and most significant bits, it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern}). \begin{itemize} \item The least significant bit can be computed as the \texttt{xor} of the three inputs. Therefore, the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set. In software, this bit sequence is represented as the integer 0b10010110 in binary or 150 in decimal. \item Computing the most significant bits involves the expression $(a \mathrm{~and~} b) \mathrm{~or~} ((a \mathrm{~xor~} b) \mathrm{~and~} c$. We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$ that can be represented as the binary string 0b11101000 or 232 in decimal. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Truth-table enumeration gives the ternary-logic immediates 150 (low bit) and 232 (high bit) for the CSA.
assumptions: it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern})
conclusions: the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set
We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$

nodes.name: \texttt{CSA\_AVX512}
nodes.statement_short: Carry-save adder over 512-bit registers using two \texttt{vpternlogd} intrinsics.

nodes.name: Most significant bits via immediate 232
nodes.statement: *h = _mm512_ternarylogic_epi32(c, b, a, 0b11101000);
nodes.statement_short: Emit the carry word with the 232 truth table.

nodes.name: Least significant bits via immediate 150
nodes.statement: *l = _mm512_ternarylogic_epi32(c, b, a, 0b10010110);
nodes.statement_short: Emit the partial-sum word with the 150 truth table.

nodes.name: Twenty-fold gain in instructions per input bit
nodes.statement: When comparing the resulting AVX-512 routine to its 64-bit equivalent (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}), we observe that the AVX-512-based CSA subroutine can process 8~times as many bits (512 versus 64) while simultaneously reducing the number of logical operations from 5 to 2. Taken together, we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits.
nodes.statement_short: 8x wider registers and 5-to-2 fewer operations give a 20x gain in instructions per input bit.
assumptions: comparing the resulting AVX-512 routine to its 64-bit equivalent (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp})
conclusions: we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits

nodes.name: Focus on 16-bit words
nodes.statement: Implementations of the positional population count depends on the desired target word size. For simplicity, we focus on 16-bit words in this work. Wider words (larger universes) can be encoded into multiple distinct streams of 16-bit words. In addition, our algorithms can be generalized to wider words without difficulty.
nodes.statement_short: All algorithms are presented for 16-bit words; wider words reduce to several 16-bit streams.

nodes.name: Scalar shift-mask-add baseline for the positional population count
nodes.statement: To compute the positional population count, we start with sixteen zero-initialized bit-counters. Next, we iterate over the bits in each word in sequence while incrementing the corresponding target bit-counter as needed. A sensible baseline algorithm for computing the positional population count involves a shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}): \begin{enumerate} \item Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient. \item Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise. \item Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: for each word and each of the 16 bit positions, shift right, mask the low bit, and add it to that position's counter.

nodes.name: Shift
nodes.statement: Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient.
nodes.statement_short: Right-shift the word by $p$.

nodes.name: Mask
nodes.statement: Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Keep only the least significant bit of the shifted word.

nodes.name: Add
nodes.statement: Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2.
nodes.statement_short: Accumulate the masked bit into counter $p$.

nodes.name: Branch misprediction behaviour of the baseline
nodes.statement: We expect this code to be compiled to efficient assembly. On superscalar processors, branches must be predicted and a branch misprediction can cost tens of cycles or more. Fortunately, in our tests, the executed code does not trigger a significant number of mispredicted branches: the end of the short loop (16) is corrected predicted.
nodes.statement_short: The 16-iteration loop is well predicted, so mispredictions do not hurt the baseline.

nodes.name: Instruction and cycle estimate for the scalar baseline
nodes.statement: For sufficiently long input streams, we estimate the number of executed instructions to $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word. Given that most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle, we expect a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}).
nodes.statement_short: The scalar baseline costs about 64 instructions and 16 cycles per 16-bit word.
assumptions: For sufficiently long input streams
most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle
conclusions: $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word
we expect a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine

nodes.name: \texttt{pospopcnt\_u16\_scalar\_basic}
nodes.statement_short: Reference C implementation: an unrolled branchless shift-mask-add over all 16 bit positions of every input word.

nodes.name: AVX-512 CSA circuit family (256\,B, 512\,B and 1\,kB blocks)
nodes.statement: We build CSA circuits over 512-bit registers using a CSA routine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csa-avx512}). The simplest network (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}) takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512-small}) and uses three calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. We can double the size of the network and process 512\,B inputs using seven calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. Again, doubling the network size, we can process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512}).
nodes.statement_short: Three CSA networks over 512-bit registers, consuming 256\,B, 512\,B or 1\,kB per iteration with 3, 7 or 15 \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} calls.

nodes.name: Simplest 256\,B network
nodes.statement: The simplest network (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}) takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512-small}) and uses three calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function.
nodes.statement_short: Build the base circuit on four registers with three CSA calls.

nodes.name: Double to a 512\,B network
nodes.statement: We can double the size of the network and process 512\,B inputs using seven calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function.
nodes.statement_short: Double the circuit width to 512\,B blocks (7 CSA calls).

nodes.name: Double again to a 1\,kB network
nodes.statement: Again, doubling the network size, we can process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512}).
nodes.statement_short: Double again to 1\,kB blocks (15 CSA calls).

nodes.name: Instructions per block for the three CSA circuits
nodes.statement: Each call to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function involves only two instructions (two times \texttt{vpternlogd}). Excluding load and store instructions, we use \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 6~instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 14~instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 30~instructions per block of 1\,kB. \end{inparaenum} Notably, the number of instructions per input volume increases with wider circuits.
nodes.statement_short: The CSA networks cost 6, 14 and 30 instructions per 256\,B, 512\,B and 1\,kB block respectively.
assumptions: Excluding load and store instructions
Each call to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function involves only two instructions (two times \texttt{vpternlogd})
conclusions: 6~instructions per block of 256\,B
14~instructions per block of 512\,B
30~instructions per block of 1\,kB

nodes.name: AVX-512 positional population count over CSA circuits
nodes.statement: At the end of each circuit, we have a set of registers \{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\} corresponding, for each bit position in $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$, to the sum of set bits. For simplicity let us assume that we are working with the smaller circuit (256\,B). Before starting the procedure, the registers \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} and the 16 output bit-counters are zero-initialized. Next, the first 512\,B of inputs are process with the circuit and receive as output the updated values of \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. In addition, we also receive a new register \texttt{B3} corresponding to the fourth least significant bit of the sum of the set bits at position $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$. We can update our sixteen bit-counters by checking the bits in \texttt{B3}: the first counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{0, 16, 32, \ldots, 496\}$, the second counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{1, 17, 33, \ldots, 497\}$, and so forth. The process of loading the next 512\,B of input data, call the circuit, and providing it with the updated values \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} is repeated until no more data is available. At this point, when no more input data is available, we must increment our bit-counters with the remaining bits in \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. These are processed as \texttt{B3} except that the multiplier is 1, 2 and 4 respectively.  The algorithms using the large circuits (512\,B and 1\,kB) work similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Run the CSA circuit over successive blocks, folding the overflow register \texttt{B3} into the sixteen bit-counters with weight 8, then flush \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} with weights 1, 2, 4.

nodes.name: Zero-initialize registers and counters
nodes.statement: Before starting the procedure, the registers \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} and the 16 output bit-counters are zero-initialized.
nodes.statement_short: Zero the bit-plane registers and the sixteen counters.

nodes.name: Process a block through the circuit
nodes.statement: Next, the first 512\,B of inputs are process with the circuit and receive as output the updated values of \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. In addition, we also receive a new register \texttt{B3} corresponding to the fourth least significant bit of the sum of the set bits at position $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$.
nodes.statement_short: Feed one block through the CSA circuit, obtaining updated $B_0,B_1,B_2$ and an overflow register $B_3$.

nodes.name: Fold \texttt{B3} into the sixteen bit-counters
nodes.statement: We can update our sixteen bit-counters by checking the bits in \texttt{B3}: the first counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{0, 16, 32, \ldots, 496\}$, the second counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{1, 17, 33, \ldots, 497\}$, and so forth.
nodes.statement_short: Add eight times each strided bit sum of $B_3$ into the corresponding positional counter.

nodes.name: Iterate over remaining blocks
nodes.statement: The process of loading the next 512\,B of input data, call the circuit, and providing it with the updated values \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} is repeated until no more data is available.
nodes.statement_short: Loop over the input stream carrying $B_0,B_1,B_2$ forward.

nodes.name: Flush the residual bit-plane registers
nodes.statement: At this point, when no more input data is available, we must increment our bit-counters with the remaining bits in \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. These are processed as \texttt{B3} except that the multiplier is 1, 2 and 4 respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Drain $B_0,B_1,B_2$ into the counters with weights 1, 2 and 4.

nodes.name: Vectorized bit-counter increment from the \texttt{B3} register
nodes.statement: The inner loop of our algorithm, where the bit-counters from the \texttt{B3} register are updated could become expensive. This loop execute 16~sums of 32~bit values and multiply the result by eight. This final multiplication can be deferred until the end of the main loop. Further, we vectorize the sum (Fig.~\ref{fig:increment-avx512}) by using sixteen vector of counters, each spanning 512~bits, or thirty-two 16-bit counters, instead of using sixteen scalar counters. Given the \texttt{B3} register, we select the least significant bit of each 16-bit word by using a mask-select operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_and_si512} intrinsic function. Next, we increment counters using a horizontal add operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_add_epi16} intrinsic. Finally, we shift each 16-bit subword of the \texttt{B3} register right by one bit with the \texttt{_mm512_srli_epi16} intrinsic function.
nodes.statement_short: Vectorize the counter update with sixteen 512-bit counter registers, using mask-select, horizontal add and right shift, deferring the multiply by eight.
output: sixteen vector of counters, each spanning 512~bits, or thirty-two 16-bit counters

nodes.name: Mask-select the least significant bit
nodes.statement: Given the \texttt{B3} register, we select the least significant bit of each 16-bit word by using a mask-select operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_and_si512} intrinsic function.
nodes.statement_short: Extract the low bit of every 16-bit lane.

nodes.name: Horizontal add into the counters
nodes.statement: Next, we increment counters using a horizontal add operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_add_epi16} intrinsic.
nodes.statement_short: Accumulate the extracted bits into the vector counters.

nodes.name: Shift the register right by one bit
nodes.statement: Finally, we shift each 16-bit subword of the \texttt{B3} register right by one bit with the \texttt{_mm512_srli_epi16} intrinsic function.
nodes.statement_short: Shift each lane right to expose the next bit position.

nodes.name: Scalar form of the counter-increment procedure
nodes.statement_short: Scalar double loop: for each of 16 positions, add the low bit of each of the 32 subwords and shift.

nodes.name: Vectorized counter increment (AVX-512)
nodes.statement_short: AVX-512 loop over the 16 bit positions: mask the low bit of each 16-bit lane, add it to the position's counter register, then shift $B$ right.

nodes.name: Build the 1-mask
nodes.statement_short: Broadcast the constant 1 into every 16-bit lane.

nodes.name: Select the least significant bits
nodes.statement: __m512i masked = _mm512_and_si512(B, one)); // Select LSB (bit) with 1-mask
nodes.statement_short: AND with the 1-mask to isolate the low bit per lane.

nodes.name: Accumulate into the position counter
nodes.statement: counter[pos]   = _mm512_add_epi1(counter[pos], masked); // Horizontal add
nodes.statement_short: Add the masked bits into counter register \texttt{pos}.

nodes.name: Shift for the next bit position
nodes.statement: B = _mm512_srli_epi16(B, 1); // Shift 16-bit words right by 1 bit
nodes.statement_short: Shift each 16-bit lane right by one bit.

nodes.name: CSA circuit processing 4 registers (256\,B)
nodes.statement_short: Three \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} calls reduce four 512-bit input registers into $B_0$, $B_1$, $B_2$.

nodes.name: CSA the first input pair into B0
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B1A , &B0  , B0  , data[i]     , data[i + 1] );
nodes.statement_short: Absorb \texttt{data[i]} and \texttt{data[i+1]} into \texttt{B0}, carry to \texttt{B1A}.

nodes.name: CSA the second input pair into B0
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B1B , &B0  , B0  , data[i + 2] , data[i + 3] );
nodes.statement_short: Absorb \texttt{data[i+2]} and \texttt{data[i+3]} into \texttt{B0}, carry to \texttt{B1B}.

nodes.name: Merge the carries into B1 and emit B2
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B2  , &B1  , B1  , B1A         , B1B         );
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two carries with \texttt{B1}, overflowing into \texttt{B2}.

nodes.name: CSA circuit processing 16 registers (1\,kB)
nodes.statement_short: Fifteen \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} calls reduce sixteen 512-bit input registers into $B_0$, $B_1$, $B_2$, $B_3$.

nodes.name: Reduce the first four inputs
nodes.statement_short: First 4-input sub-circuit, carry accumulated in \texttt{B2A}.

nodes.name: Reduce the second four inputs
nodes.statement_short: Second 4-input sub-circuit, carry accumulated in \texttt{B2B}.

nodes.name: Merge the first half into B2
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B2A. , &B2  , B2  , B2A         , B2B         );
nodes.statement_short: Combine the two half-carries into \texttt{B2}.

nodes.name: Reduce the third four inputs
nodes.statement_short: Third 4-input sub-circuit, carry accumulated in \texttt{B2A}.

nodes.name: Reduce the fourth four inputs
nodes.statement_short: Fourth 4-input sub-circuit, carry accumulated in \texttt{B2B}.

nodes.name: Merge the second half into B2
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B2B  , &B2  , B2  , B2A         , B2B         );
nodes.statement_short: Combine the remaining half-carries into \texttt{B2}.

nodes.name: Emit the overflow register B3
nodes.statement: CSA_AVX512(&B3   , &B2  , B2  , B2A         , B2B         );
nodes.statement_short: Final CSA producing the fourth bit plane \texttt{B3}.

nodes.name: Total instructions per block after unrolling the counter update
nodes.statement: By unrolling this vectorized code, we achieve $3 \times 16=48$~instructions, without considering overhead and load/store instructions. We can add these 48~instructions to our previous counts: \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 54 instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 62 instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 78~instructions per block of 1\,kB. \end{inparaenum}
nodes.statement_short: Adding the 48 unrolled counter-update instructions gives 54, 62 and 78 instructions per 256\,B, 512\,B and 1\,kB block.
assumptions: without considering overhead and load/store instructions
conclusions: 54 instructions per block of 256\,B
62 instructions per block of 512\,B
78~instructions per block of 1\,kB

nodes.name: Instructions per 16-bit word and 400-fold instruction reduction
nodes.statement: Dividing by the number of 16-bit words processed, we get the following instruction counts per word: \begin{enumerate} \item 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B, \item 0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B, and \item 0.15 when using blocks of 1\,kB. \end{enumerate} Based on these numbers, as block sizes get larger, we expect fewer instructions per input word and therefore improved performance. In comparison, we estimate about 64~instructions per 16-bit word for the scalar version. This corresponds to a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions.
nodes.statement_short: 0.42, 0.24 and 0.15 instructions per 16-bit word for the three block sizes, a $>$400-fold reduction over the scalar 64.
assumptions: we estimate about 64~instructions per 16-bit word for the scalar version
conclusions: 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B
0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B
0.15 when using blocks of 1\,kB
This corresponds to a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions

nodes.name: Fixed overhead and the 1\,kB minimum input
nodes.statement: This analysis ignores the overhead cost of recovering the counts from both the vectorized counters and the running registers $\{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\}$. For small inputs, this overhead can occupy a dominant proportion of the total cost. For example, the sixteen vector counters span 1\,kB on their own. Hence, to achieve good performance, the input stream should at least exceed 1\,kB.
nodes.statement_short: Counter-recovery overhead dominates small inputs, so inputs should exceed 1\,kB.

nodes.name: Summary of the SIMD CSA networks and residual handling
nodes.statement: Taken together, we describe several SIMD-accelerated CSA networks of different sizes for computing the positional population count with up to $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions compared to a scalar implementation. Our SIMD-based approach can compute the positional population count for inputs that are a multiple of 256\,B. Any residual input values will be processed using a scalar subroutine.
nodes.statement_short: The SIMD networks handle inputs in multiples of 256\,B; residual values fall back to the scalar subroutine.

nodes.name: Implementation and experimental platform
nodes.statement: We implemented the algorithms in C99 and we make them available online at \url{https://github.com/lemire/pospopcnt_avx512} under the Apache 2.0 license. Code was compiled with GCC 8.2 using the optimization flags \texttt{-O2 -march=native}. All tests were performed using a host machine with a Cannon Lake microarchitecture (Table~\ref{tab:test-cpus}). Performance was measured using the Linux performance counters (e.g. \texttt{PERF\_COUNT\_HW\_CPU\_CYCLES} to count processor cycles). The host processor has 32\,kB of L1 cache per core, 256\,kB of L2 cache per core and 4\,MB of L3 cache. We verified that the processor is not subject to downclocking when running AVX-512 instructions\cite{inteloptimization} using the \texttt{avx-turbo}~\cite{avxturbo} benchmarking tool.
nodes.statement_short: C99 implementation, GCC 8.2 \texttt{-O2 -march=native}, Cannon Lake host, Linux performance counters, no AVX-512 downclocking.

nodes.name: Data independence of the measured performance
nodes.statement: For all experiments, we generate random data using a Mersenne Twister pseudorandom number generator. However, we find that performance is independent of the input data as our algorithms do not branch on the content of the data.
nodes.statement_short: Random inputs; performance is data-independent because the algorithms are branchless in the data.

nodes.name: Break-even input size for the AVX-512 approach
nodes.statement: Our proposed AVX-512-based approach has a fixed overhead, irrespective of the input stream size. This overhead is non-negligible for small inputs. For tiny inputs (512~words), we need about 30~instructions per 16-bit word, and almost all of these instructions are part of the overhead. However, once we reach a few thousands words (e.g., 4096~words or 8\,kB), our AVX-512-based approach becomes beneficial.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed overhead dominates tiny inputs (30 instructions/word at 512 words) but the AVX-512 approach wins from a few thousand words onward.
assumptions: For tiny inputs (512~words)
once we reach a few thousands words (e.g., 4096~words or 8\,kB)
conclusions: we need about 30~instructions per 16-bit word, and almost all of these instructions are part of the overhead
our AVX-512-based approach becomes beneficial

nodes.name: Benchmarking protocol
nodes.statement: We simulated random input data for 8 and 512 kB, as well as 16, 64, 256, and 1024 MB and benchmarked our three different CSA circuits against a scalar implementation (Table~\ref{tab:results}). To guarantee reliability, we repeat each test three times and verify that the standard error is well within a 5\%. We also present the speeds in GB/s for input sizes up to 64\,MB (see Fig.~\ref{fig:speed}).
nodes.statement_short: Six input sizes from 8\,kB to 1\,GB, three repetitions each, standard error under 5\%.

nodes.name: Measured performance of the scalar and AVX-512 algorithms
nodes.statement: For the scalar algorithm, we observe a fixed speed over the range of inputs in our experiments: 17~cycles and 65~instructions per input word. Overall, the fastest approach is our proposed AVX-512 algorithm with large block size (1\,kB), except maybe for inputs of less than 64\,kB. Increasing the input size reduce the number of instructions per input word and simultaneously increase speed. Due to diminishing returns, the performance for 1\,GB inputs are practically identical to that of 256\,MB. In the best scenario, the AVX-512 approach uses 300~times fewer instructions compared to the scalar approach. As a reference point, the C \texttt{memcpy} function runs at a speed of 20\,GB/s for large inputs compared to 18 GB/s for the positional popcount operation on large inputs.
nodes.statement_short: Scalar costs 17 cycles / 65 instructions per word; the 1\,kB AVX-512 circuit is fastest, using 300x fewer instructions and reaching 18\,GB/s versus 20\,GB/s for \texttt{memcpy}.
assumptions: over the range of inputs in our experiments
conclusions: For the scalar algorithm, we observe a fixed speed over the range of inputs in our experiments: 17~cycles and 65~instructions per input word
the fastest approach is our proposed AVX-512 algorithm with large block size (1\,kB), except maybe for inputs of less than 64\,kB
In the best scenario, the AVX-512 approach uses 300~times fewer instructions compared to the scalar approach

nodes.name: Conclusion: near-memcpy speed and 40-fold speedup
nodes.statement: Taken together, we introduce a novel population count operation referred to as the \textit{positional population count} (\texttt{pospopcnt}) and introduce efficient SIMD-accelerated algorithms based on carry-saver add (CSA) circuits. We demonstrate that we can process 16-bit words at nearly the speed of a memory copy when AVX-512 is available and when the input size is sufficiently large (e.g., 256\,MB). Our best algorithm is over 40~times faster compared to a non-vectorized approach.
nodes.statement_short: The AVX-512 pospopcnt runs at nearly memcpy speed for large inputs and is over 40x faster than scalar code.
assumptions: when AVX-512 is available and when the input size is sufficiently large (e.g., 256\,MB)
conclusions: we can process 16-bit words at nearly the speed of a memory copy
Our best algorithm is over 40~times faster compared to a non-vectorized approach
